newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican separatists to step up armed campaign.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatists to step up armed campaign.

text.p: Corsican separatist guerrillas vowed on Wednesday to step up their armed struggle against France, accusing Prime Minister Alain Juppe of seeking to crush them by force.

The Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC), which took its bombing campaign to the French mainland in September, said it planned "new forms" of attacks on the mainland and threatened local politicians and the families of paramilitary police on the Mediterranean island.
"Since Juppe has opted for a military solution...we have decided to adapt our struggle on the ground with increased resources," the FLNC's hardline "historic wing" said.
"Our actions in France will soon take new forms," it said.
The FLNC claimed responsibility for a spectacular blast that wrecked Juppe's mayoral office in Bordeaux on October 5 as well as bombs in Marseille, Aix-en-Provence and Limoges last month.

The movement has always taken care to avoid civilian casualties but its threat added to the worries of police already on alert after a suspected Islamic fundamentalist bombing killed four people on a Paris underground train last week.
The authenticated FLNC statement, sent to news organisations in Bastia, said the Paris government had sent the DGSE espionage service, an elite anti-terror squad and marines to Corsica.

"We call on the (gendarmerie) territorial brigades to evacuate their families and stop their derisory patrols," it said, adding: "We urge those local political leaders who have called once again for repression to make their positions clear publicly within 10 days and accept the consequences."
The statement appeared timed to put Corsica on the agenda of a long-awaited television interview of President Jacques Chirac scheduled on Thursday.
Police sources said they were taking the threats seriously.

They said the guerrillas were worried that gendarmes had stepped up their search for Francois Santoni, the leader of the FLNC's legal wing Cuncolta Naziunalista, who has gone into hiding to avoid charges of carrying arms.
The recent mainland attacks came after the FLNC ended a shaky five-month truce, during which it held secret talks with government emissaries never officially acknowledged by Paris.
It has since resumed almost daily bombings against public buildings on the holiday island of 250,000 in a two-decade-old campaign to win greater autonomy from Paris.
Juppe has pledged to crack down on the guerrillas and restore order, while proposing sweeping tax breaks for Corsica as part of a plan to revive the economy, create jobs and defuse violence.

The French National Assembly last week approved a five-year development plan, costing the state three billion francs ($580 million), to grant tax breaks to businesses operating on the island in order to encourage investment.
